David set opposite him, matching rhythm without comment. The work made sense. It borrowed your brain and filled it with timing. It felt good to be able to ignore the usual tension of a trial for a bit and just do something repetitive. For a while, that was enough. Snap. Click. Turn. Hold. Routine. And yet... something itched under Dwight’s skin almost immediately. Dwight frowned against the odd ambience. A strange noise, he could understand. That kind of thing was common, if concerning in of itself. This though? This felt...weird. The basement had a quality to its silence that didn't sit right — not the comfortable quiet of a space with nobody in it, but something closer to held breath. Could always be just the generator dampening other sounds, he mused. Normally he didn’t notice that effect, but he also didn’t usually have the time to stop and listen to the area around him for long before needing to run or hide. Shaking off the eeriness, Dwight shifted his position slightly and tried to focus back on what he was doing. If he let his mind wander too much, he could miss a spark, and the killer would DEFINITELY hear a generator misfire. Even Danny couldn’t ignore that kind of a blast. The ground made an odd sound as his shoe slid across it, drawing his eye back away from the wires again. The floor felt damp beneath his shoes. Not unusual, not really, but... more than usual. Glancing down, his foot gently rippled an inch, maybe two, of stagnant water; glossy and brown-green in the anemic light. It lay so still it had filmed over, surface tension tempering it into glass. His shoes had been sitting in it long enough that his socks were already damp at the heel. He somehow hadn't noticed. The walls seemed just as saturated, a faint sheen of moisture on the concrete like the whole room was slowly exhaling — and the scent that hung on everything was low and wet and old, mold and rust and something underneath both that he didn't have a name for. The air pressed in humid and hot, and one of the nearby pipes hissed like a living thing, sending steam drifting lazily through the room. Was it always this...wet? His breath went shallow for one beat, and then he smoothed it with reason. Basements flooded. Old buildings leaked. Pressure lines failed. The Entity was many things, but OSHA- compliant was not one of them. Though there had never been a leak like this before, he was sure of that. Even at it’s worst, the preschool was run down and broken. Never... moist. The overhead light buzzed, as if agreeing with his discomfort. It didn't flicker the way the lights usually did when a generator was running — that particular feedback was almost soothing by now, a sign that the work was registering. This was a flat, lazy drone, the light steady and somehow worse for it. The sickly light somehow managed to make everything look just a little bit off. Even the opening to the pipe hallway seemed to sit at the wrong angle. Dwight glared at the hallway, generator forgotten as the wrongness seeped into his bones, his eyes snagging on a proportion that didn't resolve correctly no matter how long he looked at it. The doorframe was fine. The hallway beyond it was fine. But the relationship between them was off somehow, stretched or rotated by a degree or two in a direction that geometry didn't technically have a name for. David didn’t seem to notice. Or maybe he just didn’t care. His entire frame was steady, eyes glued on his work, hands moving with the practiced ease of someone who had done this entirely too many times. Dwight flexed his fingers and tried to keep working, but his eyes kept tracking the edges of the room. There were flickers in the lights of most trials, sure. Ambient smells and noises that were meant to set off nerves, naturally. Still... There shouldn’t be standing water. That part he was sure of. But when he squinted down, there it was: ripples, shallow and lazy. Maybe an inch, maybe more. He was still trying to find the words for it, contemplating asking if David was noticing it too, when the pipe went. The sound cracked through the basement like a gunshot — something rupturing deep in the hallway, a violent hiss of pressure releasing all at once — and David was on his feet before the echo died. A sharp inhale punched through his teeth as he spun, one hand shooting back as if to block Dwight, ready to fend off whatever was attacking. The pipe at the far end of the hallway was weeping a dark stain down the wall, and that was all. No attacker, no disaster. Just a blown pipe. He stood there for a beat, chest rising fast, then turned, half embarrassed, half bewildered, already opening his mouth to get Dwight back on task and hopefully not harassing him for being jumpy. He froze mid syllable at his teammate’s expression. Dwight wasn't looking at him. He was still staring at the pipe hallway opening, the generator humming under his idle hands, with a stillness that made David’s hair stand on end. Clearly the man had spotted something he had missed while trying to fight absolutely nothing? David followed his gaze, not seeing anything new, and turned back to the generator with an annoyed huff. This place was clearly getting to them both. Best to get the generator done and get back upstairs before their nerves went off even worse than they already are.
